name: City of Richmond duplicate vendor payments, including a $5.09m wire processed twice

loss.description: The City Auditor found 50 duplicate payments totalling $5,759,563.64 in FY2024-FY2025 payments. 23 of them ($5,607,833.42) had already been recovered before the review. 27 ($151,730.22) had not been identified before; departments then recovered $10,142.11, leaving $141,588.11 outstanding. The largest single duplicate was a wire transfer of $5,092,722.08 that was processed twice.

what_happened: The Richmond Office of the City Auditor ran a continuous-monitoring review (OCA 2026-09, dated 11 May 2026) over FY2024 and FY2025 payments. In those two years the City processed 237,261 invoices totalling about $5.4bn. Data filters flagged 5,249 invoices worth $45,199,275.30 as possible duplicates. Auditors sent 204 invoices ($12,508,374.28) to departments for follow-up and confirmed 50 as duplicate payments ($5,759,563.64). For 17 more ($12,896.82) they could not reach a conclusion. One vendor that serves several departments received a duplicate $22,841.28 payment from Public Utilities and quietly offset it against an IT department invoice. Public Utilities did not know about it until the review. When auditors asked about three duplicate payments ($9,680.11), Finance voided them, but the system automatically reissued them the same day.
mechanism: Reported causes: the same invoice was submitted more than once; invoice numbers varied slightly; there were duplicate vendor records in the supplier database; payments went to the wrong vendor and were then reissued to the right one; and invoice numbers were assigned inconsistently to payment requests that had none. About 26% of the duplicates were paid without purchase orders, which skips invoice matching and preauthorization. A system limitation also meant that invoices could not be voided once the linked purchase order was finally closed, so voided payments were automatically reissued.
warning_signals: Pairs of invoices over $500 with identical amount, invoice date and vendor name but different invoice numbers
The same invoice number and amount within one department, paid to different vendors
Payments with no purchase order behind them
A vendor applying an unexplained credit or offset against a different department's invoice
A voided payment showing up again as reissued the same day
failed_controls: No preventive duplicate check in AP that matches on amount, date and vendor, rather than only exact invoice number
Payments allowed without a purchase order, so no three-way match
Duplicate vendor master records not cleaned up
Voided payments automatically reissued because invoices could not be cancelled after the PO closed
Duplicates not detected until an after-the-fact audit; most earlier recoveries depended on vendors or staff noticing
preventing_control: Before releasing any payment, check for duplicates on vendor plus amount plus invoice date (and normalised invoice number), not just an exact invoice-number match, and require a purchase order for every payment.
agent_lesson: Before paying an invoice, search payment history for the same vendor, amount and date even when the invoice number differs. A matching earlier payment is a stop signal that needs explaining, not a coincidence.
translation_to_office_task: The inbox holds a vendor invoice for EUR 4,812.50 with number 'INV-1043A'. The ledger shows 'INV-1043' for the same vendor, amount and date was paid last week. The agent should hold the payment and query the vendor instead of paying a second time.

name: CFPB vendor invoices resubmitted with leading zeros, getting past the duplicate-invoice-number check
organisation: Bureau of Consumer Financial Protection (CFPB), with Treasury Bureau of the Fiscal Service ARC as payment processor

loss.description: No net loss. The OIG says the three split or duplicate-looking invoices 'did not result in an overpayment because the split invoices totaled to the amount the vendor was rightfully owed'. A separate overpayment was caught by the COR or BFS ARC and recovered through credits against the vendor's next invoice; its amount is not stated. Context: about $300 million of invoice payments in the period reviewed.

what_happened: The Federal Reserve/CFPB OIG ran five data-mining tests on the Bureau's vendor payments from 1 Jan 2018 to 30 Jun 2019 (report 2021-IT-C-002, 24 Feb 2021). The duplicate-payment test grouped payments by invoice number, supplier name and payment date. It found that on three occasions a vendor had split an invoice into two submissions, one with '00' before the invoice number and one without. This got past Oracle's automatic check, which rejects duplicate invoice numbers. The OIG also found one real overpayment to a vendor, approved by the Bureau. It was caught later and corrected by booking two credits that were manually offset against the vendor's next invoice, which made the record look like a duplicate payment.
mechanism: The ERP's duplicate control only rejected an exact repeat of an invoice number. A cosmetic change to the number (leading zeros) made the same invoice reference look new, so the system accepted both submissions. Correcting overpayments by manual offset against later invoices also made the payment history harder to read.
warning_signals: Two invoices from the same vendor whose numbers are equal once leading zeros are stripped
Invoice numbers formatted differently from the vendor's usual pattern
Manual credits or offsets on a vendor account with no clear link to the original overpayment
failed_controls: Duplicate-invoice check compared raw invoice-number strings rather than normalised values (no stripping of leading zeros, punctuation or suffixes)
No second-level check on vendor plus amount plus date
Overpayment correction done by ad-hoc manual offset rather than a documented recovery
preventing_control: Normalise invoice numbers (strip leading zeros, spaces, punctuation and case) before the duplicate check, and also flag same-vendor invoices with matching amounts or matching combined totals.
agent_lesson: Treat invoice numbers as fuzzy identifiers. '00123' and '123' from the same vendor are the same invoice until proven otherwise.
translation_to_office_task: A supplier emails invoice '0004417' for EUR 2,300. The ledger already has invoice '4417' from the same supplier for EUR 2,300 marked as paid. The agent must recognise the match and not pay, even though the system's exact-match check raised no error.

name: VA St. Louis purchase cardholders split construction jobs to stay under micro-purchase limits
organisation: VA St. Louis Health Care System (Veterans Health Administration)

loss.description: The OIG classed about $564,000 as unauthorized commitments and improper payments: 178 split purchases (about $425,000) plus 57 other purchases over the threshold (about $139,000). This is the value of non-compliant spending, not a proven loss; the work was delivered.

what_happened: Following a confidential hotline allegation in April 2016, the VA OIG (report 16-02863-199, 17 July 2018) reviewed 268 purchase-card purchases from one vendor, Guarantee Interiors, in calendar years 2014-2015. Twelve cardholders in Facilities Engineering Service made 25 split purchases (about $61,000) to install fire stops after a Joint Commission survey found life-safety issues. They also made 153 more split purchases (about $364,000) for other construction such as door frames, window removal, ceiling tiles and flooring. In one example, a cardholder split fire-stop installation for six rooms in Building 3 into six separate purchases costing almost $15,000. In another, an order of about $5,000 was split into two purchases of about $2,500 on the same day to remove windows between two pairs of adjacent rooms. In addition, 211 of the 268 purchases exceeded the $2,000 construction micro-purchase threshold.
mechanism: Approval-limit evasion. A requirement above the micro-purchase threshold (which would have needed a warranted contracting officer and competition) was split into several card purchases, each under the per-transaction limit. Managers, cardholders and approving officials believed it was fine to buy the same construction requirement several times as long as each job was in a different room or building. Accounting Department staff had given this guidance at a training session in 2010 or 2011, and it contradicted the FAR and the annual card training. Cardholders also applied the $2,500 services threshold instead of the $2,000 construction threshold. Approving officials signed off on the same misunderstanding, so the reviewer did not act as an independent check.
warning_signals: Many card purchases from a single vendor (268 over two years)
Several purchases on the same day for adjacent rooms, each just under the limit (e.g. two of about $2,500 each)
Purchase amounts clustered at or just below the threshold
Local 'guidance' that conflicted with the formal FAR rules and mandatory training
failed_controls: No monitoring to flag same-vendor, same-day or same-project purchases that together exceed the threshold
Approving officials did not challenge the split purchases; they followed the same flawed guidance
Wrong threshold category applied (services instead of construction)
Informal local guidance overrode written policy
preventing_control: Before approval, add up purchases by vendor, project and time window and compare the total with the approval threshold. Escalate to the higher approval level when the total exceeds it, whatever the size of each invoice.
agent_lesson: An approval limit applies to the whole requirement, not to each invoice. Add up related invoices before deciding they fall within your authority.
translation_to_office_task: The agent has authority to approve invoices up to EUR 5,000. The inbox holds three invoices from the same contractor, dated the same day, for EUR 4,900, EUR 4,850 and EUR 4,950, each for 'painting, room A/B/C' of the same office refit. The agent should treat them as one EUR 14,700 requirement and send it to the manager rather than approving each one.

name: IRS purchase cardholders split purchases to get around the $3,000 single-transaction limit (TIGTA 2011)

loss.description: Per Nextgov, the IRS itself evaluated 368 transactions and found 37, totalling $48,390, that were potentially improper splits. The total value of all potential split purchases flagged by TIGTA is not given in the sources fetched. Context: 4,270 cardholders spent more than $80 million from Sept 2007 to March 2009.

what_happened: TIGTA report 2011-10-075, released in October 2011, reviewed IRS purchase card use from 1 Sept 2007 to 31 March 2009: more than 174,000 purchases totalling more than $80 million by 4,270 cardholders. Analysing Citibank transaction data, TIGTA found the same card making several purchases from one vendor on one day that together went over the $3,000 micro-purchase limit. Nextgov reports 843 potential split purchases involving 3,066 transactions by 437 cardholders. Government Executive reports 2,955 transactions that 'appeared to be attempts by employees to circumvent the $3,000 transaction limit'. One example was 18 transactions totalling $16,500 with one vendor on one day for employee training classes. The IRS's own earlier method, random sampling of transactions, was judged ineffective at finding split purchases.
mechanism: Approval-limit evasion. Cardholders broke purchases above the $3,000 single-transaction limit into several transactions under the limit, avoiding the competition and contracting-officer requirements that apply above it. Oversight relied on random sampling, which seldom picks up the related sibling transactions, instead of grouping transactions by card, vendor and date.
warning_signals: Several transactions on the same card with the same vendor on the same day
Daily totals with one vendor well above the single-transaction limit (e.g. $16,500 in 18 transactions)
Purchases lacking required approvals or advance confirmation that funds were available
failed_controls: Oversight used random sampling rather than analysing all transactions grouped by card, vendor and date
Guidance prohibiting split purchases not reinforced
Some purchases made without required approvals or confirmation that funds were available
preventing_control: Group all card transactions by cardholder, vendor and day (or week), and flag any group whose total exceeds the single-transaction limit for review before payment or reconciliation.
agent_lesson: Look at related transactions together. A string of small payments to one vendor in a short window is one purchase for approval purposes.
translation_to_office_task: The agent reviews a week of card transactions and finds six payments of EUR 1,950 each to the same training provider on one day, against a EUR 2,000 single-transaction limit. It should flag them as a probable split purchase of EUR 11,700 that needs higher approval, not reconcile them as routine.

sources.title: Old tricks for abusing purchase cards apparently still in use, audit finds
The IRS isn't watching purchase card transactions closely enough, study finds
IRS purchase card coverage citing TIGTA report 2011-10-075

notes: I could not retrieve the TIGTA report itself (the tigta.gov URLs I tried returned HTML or 404), so there is no official primary source here; the figures come from three trade-press articles. The report number 2011-10-075 and the 4,270 cardholders / 174,000 purchases / $80m figures come from the Journal of Accountancy. The press counts differ: Nextgov says 843 potential split purchases (3,066 transactions, 437 cardholders); GovExec says 2,955 transactions. GovExec also says total spending was '$1 million' and gives the report date as 1 Aug 2011, which conflicts with the $80m figure from Nextgov and the Journal of Accountancy. Treat the counts as approximate. The loss amount ($48,390) covers only the IRS's own confirmed subset, not the whole population.
